title: Kinetiq: rowing against the tide (fictional case)
text: Kinetiq is a Danish start-up founded in 2018 that sells connected rowing machines. The machine (€2,200) has an oak-wood frame, a patented magnetic resistance flywheel (three patents) and a large screen. A subscription (€39 per month) gives access to live and on-demand classes with 25 coaches, filmed on Nordic fjords and lakes in a calm, meditative “Nordic” style, plus a community leaderboard. Machines are sold online and in selected design and furniture stores; the frame is assembled by a Taiwanese contract manufacturer that also builds equipment for several other brands, while the flywheel and software are developed in Copenhagen.

During the Covid-19 lockdowns sales of connected fitness equipment exploded: Kinetiq's sales grew fivefold between 2019 and 2021. Since gyms reopened, demand for the whole category has fallen by about 40 %, inventories have piled up and most brands cut prices or offer rental plans. Several small players went bankrupt in 2023 and 2024; investors have become cautious.

PulseRide, the market leader, sells connected bikes, treadmills and rowers, owns content studios in New York and London, has about 6 million subscribers and strong brand awareness. It cut its hardware prices by 25 % in 2024 and launched a rental plan. Apple Fitness+ offers classes for €10 per month on any device; non-connected rowing machines cost €300–800 and can be combined with free YouTube workouts. Gyms and boutique studios are booming again. Music labels licensing the soundtracks of classes have increased their fees, and a global chip shortage delayed deliveries in 2022.

Kinetiq's churn is low (1.2 % per month versus an industry average of about 3 %), and survey data show that subscribers value the coaches and the calm atmosphere more than performance metrics. Most customers are 35–55 years old, live in large apartments and value design.

CEO Mads Holm wants to relaunch growth. He plans a 20 % price cut on the main model and a new model, “Kinetiq Go”, made of plastic, priced at €799 and sold through Amazon and large sports retailers. His business plan extrapolates the growth rate of 2020–2021 to reach one million subscribers in 2027: “PulseRide reached millions of subscribers, so can we.” He also argues that the €60m factory line built in 2021 for the flywheel must now be used at full capacity: “We cannot let that investment go to waste.” The board consists of the two founders and early investors who are enthusiastic about the product; the CFO's doubts were not discussed at the last meeting, and the plan was presented as already decided.
